connection: Session 9 established the prerequisite model. This session applies it to ordered collections with observable TimeLedger examples.

concept.title: Build the behavioral model
paragraphs: The central rule is that arrays have fixed length, lists grow, and foreach consumes each element in sequence without exposing indexing mechanics.
Names and syntax matter because they communicate whether code copies, aliases, enumerates, compares, or constrains a value.

concept.title: Program to the required capability
paragraphs: A caller should not need to provide more capability than the operation consumes.
Concrete implementations remain useful at construction boundaries; interfaces and generic contracts keep consuming code focused.

concept.title: Verify cause and effect
paragraphs: The lab changes one behavior at a time and uses tests to preserve the observation.
If the prediction differs from the result, explain the language rule before continuing.

lab.objective: Add a focused TimeLedger example that demonstrates arrays, lists, and enumeration.
lab.startingCondition: Sessions 01–09 are complete and the solution builds with all existing tests passing.
steps: Read the starting test and predict the result using the session mental model.
Add src/TimeLedger.Domain/TimeEntryCollection.cs with the smallest API needed for the example.
Add tests/TimeLedger.Domain.Tests/TimeEntryCollectionTests.cs to check the important before-and-after behavior.
Run the focused tests, then run the complete Release test suite.
Review whether each parameter and return type exposes only the capability it needs.
lab.expectedBehavior: The new tests demonstrate arrays have fixed length, lists grow, and foreach consumes each element in sequence without exposing indexing mechanics; all existing behavior remains green.
lab.validation: dotnet build TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release && dotnet test TimeLedger.sln --configuration Release

postQuiz.prompt: When should a concrete collection or implementation leak into an API?

postQuiz.explanation: Expose concrete capability only when callers genuinely need it.

whatBreaks: Removing the new domain example removes the executable model for ordered collections. Removing its tests allows subtle changes to assignment, equality, enumeration, or generic contracts to pass unnoticed. Widening the API unnecessarily gives callers capabilities the operation does not need.
summary: This session established that arrays have fixed length, lists grow, and foreach consumes each element in sequence without exposing indexing mechanics. The TimeLedger example, tests, and API review turn that rule into durable engineering practice.
